what_it_does: Large language models (LLMs) process text in two phases: a 'prefill' phase that reads and encodes the entire input prompt (computationally intensive, like running many matrix multiplications in parallel) and a 'decode' phase that generates each output token one at a time (memory-intensive, because it must retrieve all the model's stored intermediate results — called the KV cache, or the model's running notes — for every new word). With very long contexts (over 100,000 tokens, roughly the length of a novel), the KV cache alone fills up a GPU's entire memory, making it impossible to run multiple users' requests simultaneously. Hybe routes prefill to powerful GPU servers and decode to separate, cheaper NPUs (Neural Processing Units — simpler, smaller AI chips) whose memory is sized just right for streaming KV data at high speed. As the GPU finishes encoding each chunk of the prompt, it immediately streams those intermediate results to the NPU rather than holding them in GPU memory, keeping GPU memory available for new requests. A scheduler coordinates the handoff dynamically. This is based on the abstract; specific latency and throughput figures need verification from the full paper.
